newsitem.title: UK: ACPC pact may deter roaster stock build -- Merrill.
newsitem.headline: ACPC pact may deter roaster stock build -- Merrill.

text.p: An accord by coffee producers to extend export curbs by a year, if honoured, would keep roaster stocks from rebuilding next season, brokerage Merrill Lynch said in a commentary.

It also said in its May 22 report on commodity market trends that last week's decision by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to extend the curbs was seen as a safe alternative to a trigger price mechanism, as some ACPC delegates had suggested.
"The ACPC instead opted for the safe alternative and that was to extend the existing pact for one more year...If abided to the impact will keep consumer stocks from rebuilding next season," it said.
At a meeting in London, the ACPC led by Brazil agreed to continue to limit the 14 members' exports to 52.75 million bags for 12 months from July 1.
The decision surprised some consumers who had expected a loosening of supply control to cool a market that has lifted prices by 80-100 percent.
Merrill analyst Judith Ganes said in the report that there were several glaring problems over introducing price trigger levels as a device to try to adjust supply to demand.
Firstly, the run-up in world prices had already drawn out any exportable quality, and some not-so-exportable beans, to the marketplace.

"So any coffee that has been held back would be of minimum quantity and questionable quality and simply would be a symbolic gesture on the pact of the producers, but not sufficient to sate the market's appetite," she said.
Secondly, assuming there was additional coffee to be exported, the producers would have to agree on the price levels.

"This would be a difficult and time-consuming task and not likely to be set in place quick enough to have any impact," she said. "By the time it was agreed to the market would probably be on the skids already."
Ganes also said that coffee drinkers were unlikely to switch to other drinks despite increases in retail prices in reaction to higher futures.
"While studies have shown consumers in the past have drank less coffee when prices are high, we think many of these arguments don't hold sway in the current environment," she said.

"The dime or even 20-cent rise in cup prices at the retail level is not likely to break the daily routine of the coffee drinker, especially those purchasing their brew at specialty coffee bars," she added. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
